Where the previous chapter dealt with selecting columns, filtering rows,
and rearranging the resulting data set,
this chapter will look into transforming data by calculating new values
and summarizing groups of rows.

As a running example through this chapter, let's have a look at the `bechdel` data,
which contains information on the famous *Bechdel test* for female representation in films:
does the film contain any scene where two women talk about something other than a man?
This might seem a very low bar, but that will turn out to be a fairly naive assumption.

Note that this dataset is a simplified version of the data published by the [538 data-driven politics blog](https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data), now sadly discontinued.
Although ABC (the new owner of 538) removed the earlier articles
(literally the day that we wrote the first version of this chapter!),
you can still read the original article using the archive.ph link:
[The Dollar-And-Cents Case Against Hollywood’s Exclusion of Women](https://archive.ph/e7xDQ).

To download and read the data, we use the built-in `download.file` function and the tidyverse `read_csv` function:

```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/bechdel.csv", "bechdel.csv")
bechdel <- read_csv("bechdel.csv")
head(bechdel)
```

::: {.challenge}
Looking at the column names and types, can you take a guess at what each column means?

Suppose we want to know whether movies with better female representation give a better return on investment. What steps would we need to take to find this answer? And what if we want to know whether female representation is improving?

Thinking ahead for the next chapter on visualization:
- what kind of plots did they use in the linked 538 article?
- What data steps would be needed to produce the numbers for these figures?
- Can you think of other useful visualizations for this data?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Columns in the bechdel data - click to expand

| Variable | Type          | Explanation                                                                              |
|----------|---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| imdb     | character     | IMDb identifier for the film                                                             |
| year     | numeric (dbl) | Year of release                                                                          |
| title    | character     | Title of the film                                                                        |
| test     | character     | Detailed Bechdel-test outcome: one of `ok`, `dubious`, `men`, `notalk`, `nowomen`, sometimes with a `-disagree` suffix when the rating was contested |
| budget   | numeric (dbl) | Production budget in US dollars (inflation-adjusted)                        |
| domestic_gross | numeric (dbl) | Domestic (US) box-office gross in US dollars (inflation-adjusted)                                            |
| foreign_gross | numeric (dbl) | International box-office gross in US dollars (inflation-adjusted)                                             |
:::


## Changing or computing values with `mutate` {#sec-mutate}

The essential tool in the data transformation toolbox is the `mutate` function.
With mutate, you can create new columns or change the values in existing columns.

For example, if we want to know whether films that pass the test have a better return on investment,
we need to compute the return on investment (dividing earnings by budget) and recode the 10 different values for `test` into a single yes or no (dummy / boolean) column.

### The `mutate()` function

The mutate function makes it easy to create new variables or to modify
existing ones.

For example, this computes the total gross earnings (international plus domestic) for each movie:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_mutate', 'demo_mutate_round', 'demo_mutate_multi', 'demo_pipeline']
library(tidyverse)
bechdel <- read_csv("data/bechdel.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_mutate
bechdel <- mutate(bechdel, gross = domestic_gross + foreign_gross)
head(bechdel)
```

(You'll notice R can display large numbers in *scientific notation*,
i.e. using `1.3e7` to mean $1.3 \times 10^7$, or 13 million.
)

The syntax of mutate is similar to that of the `filter()` and `select()`
functions introduced in the previous chapter:
The first argument is the data frame to mutate, and then any number of
additional arguments can be given to perform mutations. The mutations
themselves are *named arguments* in the form `column_name = calculation`.
The result of the calculation will then be stored in the named column,
which can either be a new column or you can overwrite an existing column.



For calculations, you can use mathematical symbols such as `+`, `/`
(division), and `*` (multiplication). There are also many useful
functions that you can use in calculations, such as `round()` to round
values, `floor()` to round values down to the nearest whole number,
 or `abs()` to take the absolute (positive) value of numbers.

For example, we could round the budget to millions of dollars:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_mutate_round
bechdel <- mutate(bechdel, budget = round(budget / 1000000, 1))
head(bechdel)
```

Note that where the previous example created a *new* column by assigning
to a column name that was not yet in the data,
this directly *modifies* the existing budget column by re-assigning it to an existing name.


### Chaining calculations and calculating multiple values

Note that you can calculate multiple columns at the same time.
For example, you can compute the total gross
and round both gross income and budget to millions of dollars:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_mutate_multi
bechdel_recoded <- mutate(bechdel,
    gross = domestic_gross + foreign_gross,
    gross = round(gross / 1000000, digits=1),
    budget = round(budget / 1000000, digits=1)
)
head(bechdel_recoded)
```

Three things to note here. First, we assign the result of the mutate to a new object, `bechdel_recoded`,
which means that this is a new copy of the data and the original `bechdel` will also still be available.
Second, we added an extra `digits=1` option to the round function.
Lastly, note also that the second line computes `gross`, and the third line than
modifies this newly computed value.
In general, you can use the result of previous calculations directly within the same mutate function.

::: {.callout-tip title="Common error: Closing brackets and R/RStudio prompts"}

The example above included a multi-line mutate statement.
More complex and longer statements will be quite common as your code becomes more sophisticated.
One danger is that you may forget the closing parenthesis (`)`).

In the online interactive prompts, this will lead to a somewhat understandable error message:
 `unexpected end of input` -- the input ended, but R was still expecting a closing bracket.

If you run an include chunk of code in Rstudio / R, however, it will not give an error message but instead you will see that the prompt changes from `>` to `+`:

```
> mutate(bechdel, budget = round(budget / 1000000, 1)
+
```

What the `+` means is that R is still waiting for you to close a parenthesis or a quoted text.
You can give many extra commands after this, but it will patiently wait for you to close the parenthesis before actually running all of them.

So, when R feels unresponsive, check that it actually gives a `>` prompt.
If it shows an unexpected `+` prompt,  you can click to  activate the console window,
press Escape to cancel the current command, and fix and restart the command that was causing trouble.
:::

## Recoding values {#sec-recoding}

So far we've used mutate to calculate new values from old ones. Its other major job is recoding — turning the values in a column into different values. Recoding shows up constantly: collapsing many categories into a few, binning a continuous variable into ranges, or flipping cryptic codes into readable labels. R offers a few different functions for this, depending on what shape the recoding takes.

### Recoding into two options with `if_else`

The `if_else` function checks a condition for each row, and chooses one value if it's true, or an alternative value if it's false. For example, we can check whether the gross income of a film was higher than it's budget, and designate that it made a *profit* if so, and a *loss* otherwise:

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['demo_ifelse', 'demo_recode', 'demo_recode2', 'demo_casewhen', 'demo_casewhen2']
library(tidyverse)
bechdel <- read_csv("data/bechdel.csv") |>
  mutate(gross = domestic_gross + foreign_gross)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_ifelse
bechdel <- mutate(bechdel, result=if_else(gross > budget, "profit", "loss"))
head(bechdel)
```


Second, the syntax of `if_else` is `if_else(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)`.
So, the first argument (`gross > budget`) tells R to check for each row whether the `gross` column is larger than `budget`. Then, if it is true the second argument will be chosen (`profit`),
while for rows where it is false the third argument is chosen (`loss`)

An important things to note here is that the `if_else` function is used **within mutate**.
This is generally true for the functions in this chapter: `if_else` computes a value,
and `mutate` places that value in the data frame.

### Recoding multiple values with `recode_values` and `replace_values`

Next, let's consider the use case of recoding multiple values.
For example, the `bechdel` data set contains a `test` column, with 10 different values:
5 possible test outcomes (`nowomen`, `notalk`, `men`, `dubious`, and `ok`),
where each outcome can have `-disagree` appended to show that there was substantial disagreement
among the (crowd) coders this column was based on.

We can use the `recode_values` function to recode each `test` value into a new value with a more descriptive name:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_recode

bechdel <- mutate(bechdel, outcome = recode_values(test,
  "nowomen" ~ "Fewer than two named women in the film",
  "nowomen-disagree" ~ "Fewer than two named women in the film (disputed)",
  "notalk" ~ "No women talking to each other",
  "notalk-disagree" ~ "No women talking to each other (disputed)",
  "men" ~ "Women only talk to each other about men",
  "men-disagree" ~ "Women only talk to each other about men (disputed)",
  "dubious" ~ "Unclear whether the film passes the test",
  "dubious-disagree" ~ "Unclear whether the film passes the test (disputed)",
  "ok" ~ "The film passes the Bechdel test",
  "ok-disagree" ~ "The film passes the Bechdel test (disputed)"
))

# (Note: Using `select` to show only the relevant columns)
head(select(bechdel, title, test, outcome))
```

Please take a second to look at the slightly odd syntax of `recode_values`.
Its first argument is the input column (`test`).
This is followed by a series of arguments of the form `old_value ~ new_value`,
where you can read the tilde (`~`) as a kind of arrow: `old ⤳ new`.
So, you can specify as many recode rules as you need.


If multiple recode rules have the same target value,
you don't need to make a separate rule for each input.
You can also specify more than one input value to replace
by using the `c()` function to *combine* multiple values.
For example, if we wish to drop the distinction between disputed and undisputed codings, we could do:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_recode2

bechdel <- mutate(bechdel, outcome2 = recode_values(test,
  c("nowomen", "nowomen-disagree") ~ "Fewer than two named women in the film",
  c("notalk", "notalk-disagree") ~ "No women talking to each other",
  c("men", "men-disagree") ~ "Women only talk to each other about men",
  c("dubious", "dubious-disagree") ~ "Unclear whether the film passes the test",
  c("ok", "ok-disagree") ~ "The film passes the Bechdel test"
))
head(select(bechdel, title, test, outcome2))
```

As briefly mentioned above, `recode_values` has a sister function `replace_values`.
The difference between the two is what happens if you don't specify all possible input values.
In the case of `replace_values`, unnamed values are left unchanged.
In contrast, `recode_values` will turn them into missing values (`NA`),
unless an optional argument `default="Some value"` is given, in
which case that value is used instead.


::: {.callout-tip title="Package versions and updating packages"}
In this section we used the `recode_values` function.
This function was introduced in `dplyr` version 1.2, released in April 2026.

If you run this on your own computer (e.g. in RStudio) and get an error `could not find function "recode_values"`, it's possible that you have an older version of dplyr.

In general, to check what version of a package you have installed you can use:

```r
> packageVersion("dplyr")
[1] ‘1.2.1’
```

If you have a version below 1.2, you should either upgrade it or use the older function `case_match` (which is very similar to `recode_values`).
To upgrade a specific package, you can use the `install.packages` code that you probably
already used to install tidyverse initially.
You can also use `update.packages(ask=FALSE)` to update *all* packages that have an available update.
However, it is a good idea to restart R before upgrading packages,
as (especially on Windows) it can be problematic to upgrade a package that is already loaded.
So, the procedure is:

1. Save your current script(s)
2. Restart the R session (Session → Restart R)
3. Update some or all packages: `install.packages("dplyr", dependencies=TRUE)` or `update.packages(ask=FALSE)`

After this, you can run `packageVersion("dplyr")` again to see whether the new version is installed.

Note that on restarting R, by default R will save and load your 'environment',
that is the data you have currently loaded in memory.
This feels convenient, but we **strongly advise you to disable saving the environment**.
Go into Tools → Global Options, uncheck `Restore .RData into workspace at startup` and set `Save workspace to .RData on exit` to Never.

This can prevent problems with automatically re-loading packages on restarting R,
but more importantly it is better 'code hygiene': you want the results of your script
to only reflect the actual commands in the script, and not be dependent on data you have loaded in your environment.

Note that for more serious package management,
advanced users might want to look at `renv` for per-project package management,
and/or `pak` for more sophisticated dependency management.
:::

### Arbitrary recoding with `case_when`

`recode_values` allowed us to create recode rules by specifying `old ⤳ new` pairs.
Sometimes, however, there is no clear 1:1 mapping between old and new,
especially when dealing with continuous ranges or comparisons involving multiple columns.

For a simple example let's start with the task of recoding the year into periods:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_casewhen
bechdel_decade <- mutate(bechdel, decade = case_when(
  year < 1980 ~ 1970,
  year < 1990 ~ 1980,
  year < 2000 ~ 1990,
  year < 2010 ~ 2000,
  .default = 2010
))
head(bechdel_decade)
```

Again, take a minute to look at the syntax of `case_when`,
as it is similar to, but also slightly different from `recode_values`:

1. First, `case_when` has no separate input column argument, jumping directly to the recode rules which include the column name(s) in their conditions.
2. Second, the recode rules take arbitrary conditions, such as the
   `year < 1980` condition, rather than specifying only the input value.
   This makes the conditions a bit more verbose as you repeat the column name,
   but do offer the flexibility of using more powerful expressions,
   such as the comparisons used above.
3. Third, `case_when` will evaluate the rules in the order given. So, if `year < 1980`
   it will return 1970, even if the next condition (`year < 1990`) also matches.
4. Finally, like `recode_values` it accepts a `.default=` argument which is used
   if none of the rules match, but confusingly it's called `.default=` here,
   and `default=` for `recode_values`

Note that the example above shows only a relatively simple application of `case_when`
(and frankly one that could be replaced easily by a `recode_values`).
The real power of `case_when` lies in its ability to use multiple columns and
conditions that cannot be simply expressed as discrete values.

For a more complicated example, let's classify movies into `big-budget success`,
`big-budget flop`, `indie success`, and `indie flop`:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_casewhen2
bechdel <- mutate(bechdel,
  gross = domestic_gross + foreign_gross,
  roi = gross / budget,
  category = case_when(
    budget > 50000000 & roi > 1 ~ "big-budget success",
    budget > 50000000 ~ "big-budget flop",
    roi > 1  ~ "indie success",
    .default = "indie flop"
    ))
head(select(bechdel, year, title, budget, gross, roi, category))
```

Again, have a careful look at the code above.
It features three new columns that all build on each other (`gross`, `roi`, and `category`).
In the `case_when` rules, it combines comparisons of the budget and the roi:

1. First, a high budget and `roi > 1` is coded as a 'big-budget success'.
2. The next rule codes any other film with a high budget as a 'big-budget flop': a check for `roi <= 1` is not needed as these would have been matched by the first rule.
3. Then, it codes every remaining profit-making film as an 'indie success', as all high budget films are already coded by the first two rules.
4. Finally, all remaining films must be 'indie flops', as all other categories are already coded.

::: {.callout-tip title="When to use which recode function?"}

This section introduced three different recode functions, each with their own use case.
Like a carpenter with different tools in their box, you should choose the most appropriate tool
for a specific use case. To help, the table below summarizes the three functions:

| Function | Description | Use case |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| `if_else(cond, yes, no)` | Returns `yes` where `cond` is `TRUE`, `no` otherwise | Binary outcomes (pass/fail, profit/loss) |
| `recode_values(x, old ~ new, ...)` | Replaces specific input values with specific output values | One-to-one or many-to-one value substitution for categorical data |
| `case_when(cond ~ result, ..., .default = ...)` | Evaluates rules top-to-bottom, returns the result of the first matching condition | Multi-way recoding based on conditions — ranges, thresholds, multi-column logic |

R being R, there are of course many more functions for recoding.
However, we suggest using the newer `recode_values` instead of `recode` or `case_match` (unless you're stuck on an old R version), as the newer function is a clear improvement over the older functions. Similarly, avoid the built-in `ifelse` function in favor of tidyverse's `if_else` (with the underscore `_`) function: the functions are generally the same, but `if_else` avoids some serious (but rare) problems with data types, for example when dealing with date/time values.
:::

## Grouping and summarizing data {#sec-summarize}

So far, all transformations have worked on individual rows.
For many questions, however, we want to compute values for **groups of rows**.
For example, what is the average `roi` for films that pass the Bechdel test compared to films that don't?

### Summarizing data with `group_by` and `summarize`

Using the functions `group_by()` and `summarize()` we can anwer this question quite directly:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ['demo_summarize','demo_summarize_piped']
#| setup: true
library(tidyverse)
bechdel <- read_csv("data/bechdel.csv") |>
  mutate(
    roi = (domestic_gross + foreign_gross) / budget,
    passed = if_else(test %in% c("ok", "ok-disagree"), "passed", "not passed")
  )
```
```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_summarize
bechdel_grouped <- group_by(bechdel, passed)
bechdel_summary <- summarize(bechdel_grouped, mean_roi = mean(roi, na.rm=TRUE))
bechdel_summary
```

The code above consists of two steps.
In the first step, the data is **grouped by** passed.
This doesn't make any change in the data itself,
but prepares for the next step by defining the two groups of interest.

The second step takes the grouped data (`bechdel_grouped`)
and uses the `summarize` function.
Syntactically, this function looks identical to the `mutate` function:
you specify `column = calculation`, and it puts the result of the calculation in the named column.

The big difference is that `summarize` computes a single value for each **group** of rows: in this case, it computes the `mean` of the `roi` values (setting `na.rm=TRUE` to ignore any missing values).

As you can see from the result, summarize produces a radically smaller data frame than the original, which had 7 columns and almost 1,800 rows.
In fact summarize will always create a data frame with one row per group (in this case, `passed` and `not passed`), and keeps only the grouping columns (`passed`) and the columns with the summary values (`mean_roi`).

Substantively, it seems that films that pass the Bechdel test actually have a lower return on investment than films that don't.
Surprisingly, this seems to go against the conclusions of the [original article](https://archive.ph/e7xDQ).
We'll dive into this in more detail later, but first we need to introduce a new piece of syntax.

### Pipelines: The `|>` operator

The example above used two functions (`group_by` and `summarize`),
and the output (result) of the first function was used as the input (first argument) of the next function.
This essentially creates a 'pipeline' of operations that are applied to the data.

Since this is so common, R has introduced a special operator to make this more convenient: the pipeline operator `|>`.
Let's rewrite the code above with this new operator:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_summarize_piped
bechdel_summary <- bechdel |>
  group_by(passed) |>
  summarize(mean_roi = mean(roi, na.rm=TRUE))
bechdel_summary
```

As you see, the two statements are now 'chained' together in a single pipeline: the `bechdel` data is piped into the `group_by` function, and the result of the grouping is piped into `summarize`.

The biggest advantage of this is that it removes the awkward intermediate objects `bechdel_grouped`, and it saves having to type the name of the data set for every function.

We introduce this notation with `group_by() |> summarize()` because these functions form a natural pair, but note that almost all tidyverse functions can be chained together in a pipe like this.

It is important to stress that there is absolutely no difference in the end whether you use the pipeline notation or use separate statements for each step.
However, since data processing and analysis very often boils down to a sequence of steps (like read data, filtering it, computing values, and visualizing the result),
pipelines are a very natural way to capture this.
So, regardless of whether you use the notation, it is important that you are able to read it.

One last important thing to note is that `|>` was introduced as a base R feature in 2021. Before that, tidyverse shipped with its own pipeline operator, `%>%`.
For all our concerns, the two operators are identical, and there is no reason to use the older operator anymore.
However, you will find many examples on the Internet still use `%>%`, and probably as a result code generated by AI also tends to use it.
So, if you see `%>%` being used just mentally translate to `|>`, and you should stick to `|>` in your own code.

### Improving the film analysis pipeline

When we first calculated the mean ROI grouped by test outcome,
we were surprised to find that passing the test was actually a negative predictor of return on investment, contrary to the claim made in the [original 538 article](https://archive.ph/e7xDQ).
Also, if you are familiar with the film industry,
you would also have noted that returns on investment in the 8-11 range are very atypical: most films are happy to make a small profit,
but films earning many times their budget are quite exceptional
(and statistically should probably be seen as outliers!)

To improve our analysis and get closer to the last figure of the article (*Dollars Earned for Every Dollar Spent*), we should make three changes to our analysis:

1. We should use the *median* rather than the *mean* ROI, which is much less sensitive to outliers
2. We should filter on films from 1990-2013 (as that is what they used)
3. We should categorize 'dubious' films as passing the test, and split between domestic and foreign ROI.

Using the pipeline syntax introduced above, we can make a single analysis pipeline that performs all these steps correctly:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_pipeline

bechdel |>
  filter(year >= 1990, year <= 2013) |>
  mutate(roi_domestic = domestic_gross / budget,
         roi_foreign = foreign_gross / budget,
         test5 = str_remove(test, "-disagree"),
         outcome = recode_values(test5,
           c("ok", "dubious") ~ "1 Passes Bechdel Test",
           "men" ~ "2 Women only talk about men",
           "notalk" ~ "3 Women don't talk to each other",
           "nowomen" ~ "4 Fewer than two women")) |>
  group_by(outcome) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            roi_domestic = median(roi_domestic, na.rm=TRUE),
            roi_foreign = median(roi_foreign, na.rm=TRUE))
```

This gives quite a different picture!
The numbers are now much more realistic, with up to 37% median profit
rather than the earlier exaggerated means.
More importantly, the numbers now match the outcome of the 538 article:
Films that pass the Bechdel test actually perform **better** in the US (and Canada, which is considered domestic), while performing similarly in the foreign market.
This shows the importance of using the right summary statistic (as well as of preprocessing decisions).

Some things to note about this code:

- Similar to `mutate`, we create multiple columns in the `summarize` call by passing named arguments, `n=`, `roi_domestic=` and `roi_foreign=`
- We used `n=n()` to add the total amount of cases per group. This is a very useful function, but it can be confusing since it doesn't take any arguments - it just counts the number of rows in each group.
- We don't store the result in an object, but only display it on the screen. If you want to continue analysing the summary result, you can simply assign it to an object like any other.
- We use `str_remove(test, "-disagree")` to remove the `-disagree` suffix from the test column, see @sec-stringr for an in-depth discussion of text handling
- We prefix the outcomes with a number (1 to 4) to make the alphabetic sorting match the natural ordering. See @sec-factor for a more elegant solution

### Adding group statistics with `group_by |> mutate` {#sec-groupbymutate}

Above we used `group_by |> summarize`, which replaced the current
data set by a summary frame containing only one row per group
and dropping all columns except for the group identifiers and summary columns.

Although `group_by` is often paired with `summarize`,
you can also follow it with a `mutate` call.

For example, using the `decade` column calculated earlier,
we can calculate the average budget of films per decade:


```{webr}
#| exercise: ['demo_groupby_mutate', 'demo_groupby_mutate2', 'demo_groupby_slice']
#| setup: true
library(tidyverse)
bechdel_decade <- read_csv("data/bechdel.csv") |>
  mutate(decade = case_when(
    year < 1980 ~ 1970,
    year < 1990 ~ 1980,
    year < 2000 ~ 1990,
    year < 2010 ~ 2000,
    .default = 2010
))

```
```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_groupby_mutate
bechdel_budget_decade <- bechdel_decade |>
  select(imdb, year, decade, title, test, budget) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  mutate(mean_budget = mean(budget, na.rm=TRUE))
head(bechdel_budget_decade)
```

Two things to notice. First: rather than replacing the data frame with the summary values, `group_by |> mutate` **added** the summary values to the existing data set. Second, the values for `mean_budget` are repeated for the top six rows. In fact, the mean budget in that decade will be repeated for each row in each decade. In that sense, `group_by |> mutate` is very close to a normal `mutate` call, in the sense that it just adds (or replaces) the specified columns, leaving the rest of the data alone.
What is special about the `group_by` is that any summary values used in the subsequent mutate are not calculated over the whole data set, but are calculated for each group: in this case the mean budget per decade.

It might seem strange to repeat a value like this,
but it is really useful in cases where you want to compare individual rows to the group statistic.
For example, we could see which films had a relatively high budget compared to other films in that decade:


```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_groupby_mutate2
bechdel_decade |>
  select(imdb, year, decade, title, test, budget) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  mutate(mean_budget = mean(budget, na.rm=TRUE),
         relative_budget = budget / mean_budget) |>
  arrange(desc(relative_budget)) |>
  head()
```

As you can see, Avatar was the film with the most exceptionally high budget, having cost more than 8 times the average film in that decade.
Interestingly, this top-6 of (relatively) exceptionally expensive movies is a decent list of well known blockbusters, with the possible exception of Shaft (1971) - but admittedly the authors of this book weren't around back then.

Note that the list of relatively expensive movies is not saved as an object here -- it is piped to `head()`, printing the top 6 rows on the screen for inspection without saving it.

### Selecting items with `slice_*`   {#sec-groupbyslice}

A final useful operation on groups is to `slice` them,
for example to take the highest grossing film per decade:

```{webr}
#| exercise: demo_groupby_slice
highestgross_per_decade <- bechdel_decade |>
  mutate(gross=domestic_gross + foreign_gross) |> 
  group_by(decade) |>
  slice_max(order_by=gross, n=1, with_ties=TRUE)
highestgross_per_decade |>
  select(decade, year, title, gross)
```
::: {.challenge}
- Do those films make sense to you? 
- It seems odd that the 2010s had a relatively low highest grossing film. What could cause this? How can you check this in the data?
  (hint: try changing decade to year in the code above, and then adding `|> print(n=100)` after the select to print all rows)
- How do `slice` and `group_by` interact? What would happened if you `slice` without a `group_by`?
:::

The code above takes a *slice* for each group, in this case taking the single (`n=1`)
row with the highest gross within that decade. 
The `with_ties=TRUE` (which is also the default) means that in the unlikely case that two films had identical gross,
it would keep both rather than only selecting the first - set it to `FALSE` to ensure you get only a single row per group.

Besides `slice_max` and its companion `slice_min`, 
you can also use `slice_head` or `slice_tail` to select the first or last row(s) in each group
(especially useful if the data is already ordered); and `slice_sample` to take a random sample of rows from each group
(useful for stratified samples).

## Column types: texts, numbers, and dates {#sec-column-types}

In R, every object and column has a data *type*,
for example `character` (for textual data) or `numeric` (confusingly abbreviated to `<dbl>` because internally it's stored with 'double' precision). 
This type is very important in determining how data is handled
and what operations are possible. 
For example, you can add numbers together but not texts.

In most cases, R will automatically detect the type when you load 
a file. For example, `read_csv` reads the first 1,000 rows of a file
and then guesses the right column type. 

In some cases, however, you might want to change this yourself.
Consider the following dataset of US county-level demographics:

```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/us-counties.csv", "us-counties.csv")
counties <- read_csv("us-counties.csv")
head(counties)
```

As you can see, this has a 5-digit `fips` (Federal Information Processing Standards) code identifying each county. In this case, it is ingested as a character (`<chr>`) column because it starts with a 0 (which would be lost as a number, since `01001` and `1001` are the same numerical value). 

Now, you could change this default in `read_csv`: try adding `col_types = list(fips="numeric")` as an argument to `read_csv` in the code above, and checking whether the column type changed to numeric (`<dbl>`). 

However, you can also change column types in a mutate call. For example, the following will change the character column to a numeric column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ['asnumeric', 'ascharacter', 'ascharacter2', 'formatdigits', 'scales']
#| setup: true
library(tidyverse)
counties <- read_csv("data/us-counties.csv")
counties_num <- mutate(counties, fips = as.numeric(fips))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: 'asnumeric'
counties_num <- mutate(counties, fips = as.numeric(fips))
head(counties_num)
```

Similarly, you could use `as.character` to turn it back into a textual column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: 'ascharacter'
mutate(counties_num, fips = as.character(fips))
```

However, this of course does not bring back the leading zero. 
For this, we can use the `str_pad` function to 'pad' a 'string' to a given length. Try replacing `as.character` in the code above with `str_pad(fips, width=5, pad = "0")`. Note that `str_pad` is part of the `stringr` package for dealing with textual data, which will be covered in @sec-stringr for more details. 

### Formatting numbers

Now suppose we want to display the column `nonwhite_pct` as a textual percentage.
We could use `as.character` to convert it to a character column:

```{webr}
#| exercise: 'ascharacter2'
mutate(counties, nonwhite_pct = as.character(nonwhite_pct))
```

However, this mostly shows that the number is internally stored with way more decimals than we will ever need (and probably also more than warranted by the actual measurement precision). 
We could use the format function to set the number of digits:

```{webr}
#| exercise: 'formatdigits'
mutate(counties, nonwhite_pct = format(nonwhite_pct, digits=2))
```

Interestingly, this works but gives a single decimal digit for the percentages.
The reason for that is that `digits` specifies the minimum number of *significant digits*, rather than the number of decimal places. 

The easiest way to achieve a fixed number of decimal places is to use the
`number()` function from the `scales` packages, which is included when you installed
tidyverse but not loaded by default:


```{webr}
#| exercise: 'scales'
library(scales)
mutate(counties, nonwhite_pct = number(nonwhite_pct, accuracy=.01, suffix="%"))
```

## Working with Dates and Times

Many data sets in social science research have a temporal dimension:
(social) media coverage of a campaign or issue changing over time; 
yearly or even daily economic indicators; panel survey responses per week or per year. 

Working with such data requires handling date or date+time columns. 
For example, let's look at a dataset of Bluesky posts around the Brazilian 2024
elections (see [the book's github repository](https://github.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/blob/main/data/README.md#brazilian-bluesky-posts) for the R code used to scrape these posts):

```{webr}
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vanatteveldt/r4css/refs/heads/main/data/bluesky_brazil_elections_2024.csv", "bluesky_brazil_elections_2024.csv")
posts <- read_csv("bluesky_brazil_elections_2024.csv")
head(posts)
```
```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['wday', 'floor_date', 'formatdate', 'dmy', 'mdy_hm', 'ggplotdate', 'with_tz', 'difftime']
library(tidyverse)
posts <- read_csv("data/bluesky_brazil_elections_2024.csv")
formatted <- posts |> 
  mutate(prettydate=format(created_at, format="%A, %d %B %Y")) |>
  select(created_at, prettydate, text)
```


As you can see, this dataset includes a row for every post, which have a `created_at` and `indexed_at` column, 
representing the timestamp they were created by the user's client and indexed by the bluesky server, respectively.
Both columns are automatically recognized and parsed as timestamps (`dttm` means date and time).

### Extracting parts of a date

When working with dates or timestamps, you commonly want to do things such as calculating the day of week,
or grouping events by day, week, or month. 
This is made very easy with functions from the `lubridate` package (see the [cheat sheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/lubridate.pdf)).
For example, we can use `wday` to calculate the day of the week for each post,
and see on which days people posted the most:

```{webr}
#| exercise: wday
posts |> 
  mutate(weekday=wday(created_at, label=TRUE)) |>
  group_by(weekday) |>
  tally()
```


Other extraction functions include `date` (to strip the time part), `year`, `quarter`, `month`, etc. 

::: {.challenge title="Subtracting dates"}
Besides using functions to extract part of a date,
you can also subtract two dates to calculate the difference.
As noted, the `posts` data frame has an `indexed_at` column as well as a `created_at` column.

- Can you compute a new column to calculate this difference? What does this number mean substantively?
- What is the `class()` of this column? What happens if you convert it to numeric?
- `as.numeric` has a `units=` option for time differences. What changes if you set it to `units="mins"`? 
  (note, see `?difftime` for more information on this)
- Finally, can you make a histogram of time differences. Do they make sense?

You can use the empty chunk below to test and run code:

```{webr}
#| exercise: difftime
head(posts)
```
:::

### Grouping dates and timestamps with `floor_date`

Besides the extraction functions mentioned above, a very useful function is `floor_date`. 
This function 'rounds down' a date to the start of a period such as year, quarter, day, or hour. 
This allows you to easily group posts (or other items) that were created in the same quarter or day.
For example, the code below shows the number of posts per month:

```{webr}
#| exercise: floor_date
posts |>
  mutate(month=floor_date(created_at, unit="month")) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  tally()
```

Note that rounding down to the month is quite different from extracting the month:
`month(as.Date("2024-04-17"))` will return 4 (the month number), 
while `floor_date(as.Date("2024-04-17"), unit="month")` will return "2024-04-01", i.e. the first date of that particular month.
So, if you want to know if people post more in the evening or in the morning, you want to extract the hour using `hour()`,
since that will pool all posts at the same hour, regardless of the day.
If you want to make an hourly timeline of posts over multiple days, you should use `floor_date(unit="hour")`,
which returns distinct hours for each day.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="On week numbers"}

For some applications, weeks are the most logical unit of analysis. 
Many activities, including work, leisure, and (social) media production and consumption follow weekly patterns.
When aggregating per month, for example, some months will have four weekends while other months have five,
which can make a big difference for looking at sporting, dating, but also religious activities. 

A possible issue here is that years don't always start on a Monday, so weeks can be spread over two calendar years,
but of course we would like every week to have seven days. 
Using `floor_date` on weeks is safe, as every date will be 'rounded down' to the previous Sunday (or Monday, if you set `week_start=1`).
Wednesday, January 1st will simply be changed to Sunday 29 December of the previous year.

When calculating the week number for a given date, however, it becomes more complicated.
The `week()` function will simply start the first week on January first running to January 7, regardless of the day of week.
Although simple, this means that the weeks won't always start on a Monday (or Sunday), which is generally not how we think of weeks.

The most standardized solution is to use ISO weeks, named after the ISO 8601 standard which defines week 1 of a year as the first Monday-Sunday
week with at least four days in it. So, if January 1st is a Friday (or Saturday or Sunday), it will be seen as part of the last week of the previous year,
while if the year starts on a Thursday (or Monday-Wednesday) this will be week 1, and the last days of the previous year are also seen as part of that week.

The advantage of this is that every week is a full Monday-Sunday week, but the price is that some days belong to a week from a different calendar year. 
For this reason, the `isoyear` function provides the year that corresponds to the week number,
so for Friday January 1st the `isoyear` will be the previous calendar year.

To see this in action, the following code shows the `isoyear` and `isoweek` for the last and first day of two years:

```{webr}
tibble(date=c("2008-12-31", "2009-01-01", "2009-12-31", "2010-01-01")) |>
  mutate(weekday=wday(date, label=TRUE), year=year(date), 
         isoyear=isoyear(date), isoweek=isoweek(date))
```

Note that while `floor_date(unit="week")` by default assumes a week starting on Sunday, the ISO standard defines weeks as starting on Monday.
If this is a problem, you can use `floor_date(unit="week", week_start=1)` to tell `floor_date` to start on Mondays.
Alternatively, there is a related pair of functions, `epiweek` and `epiyear`, which give the epidemiological week: this is a very similar standard to `isoweek`, but starts the week on Sunday rather than Monday. 
:::



### Parsing and formatting dates

In the example above, the timestamps were automatically recognized as such and parsed by R,
either implicly (e.g. when reading data in `read_csv`) or explictly (e.g. in `as.Date("2024-01-01")`)
The reason for this is that they were all given in the unambiguous ISO standard notation:
`"2024-04-17"` for a simple date, or `"2024-12-16T18:42:03Z"` for a timestamp.
In general, this is the preferred format for dates and times: 
First, it is not ambiguous in the way `4/7/76` is (is it fourth of July or April 7? And how sure are you that it's 1976?).
Additionally, since it goes from largest to smallest unit, it sorts properly using alphabetic sorting.

However, in many cases we will have to use data which is produced with a national standard, 
and we might want to label graphs with dates that are more readable to a specific audience. 

To format dates, the best option is the `format` function:

```{webr}
#| exercise: formatdate
formatted <- posts |> 
  mutate(prettydate=format(created_at, format="%A, %d %B %Y")) |>
  select(created_at, prettydate, text)
head(formatted)
```

As you can see, the function takes a `format` parameter. This parameter gives the template to be used for formatting the dates,
and can include literal characters (such as `,` or `-`) as well as `%`-placeholders for the year, month, et cetera.
The table below gives a list of the most commonly used placeholders:

| Code | Meaning                  | Example (for 2024-04-07 18:42:03) |
|------|--------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `%Y` | Year, four digits        | 2024                              |
| `%y` | Year, two digits         | 24                                |
| `%m` | Month number             | 04                                |
| `%B` | Month name               | April                             |
| `%b` | Month name, abbreviated  | Apr                               |
| `%d` | Day of the month         | 07                                |
| `%A` | Weekday name             | Sunday                            |
| `%a` | Weekday, abbreviated     | Sun                               |
| `%H` | Hour (24-hour clock)     | 18                                |
| `%M` | Minute                   | 42                                |
| `%S` | Second                   | 03                                |

: Common date and time format codes {#tbl-format-codes}

To parse dates, the easiest option is to use the parsing functions that are shipped with `lubridate`.
These functions tell R the order of fields to read, and R takes care of the rest.
So, to parse the `prettydate` column we created earlier, we use the
`dmy` function since the field is formatted day-month-year:

```{webr}
#| exercise: dmy
formatted |> 
  mutate(parsed = dmy(prettydate))
```

As you can see, this re-parses the date part of the original timestamp and deals with 
the fact that the month is given as a name automatically 
(but see the note below on languages for month and week names).
Similar functions are included for parsing timestamps. 
The example below shows how the date is `format`ted using American m/d/y notation with time included,
and then parsed using `mdy_hm` (month-day-year_hour-minute):

```{webr}
#| exercise: mdy_hm

posts |> 
  select(created_at) |>
  mutate(timestamp=format(created_at, format="%m/%d/%Y %H:%M"),
         parsed=mdy_hm(timestamp))
```

### Time zones

As a final complication, timestamps in R are always associated with a time zone.
In the CSV file we used for the Brazilian Bluesky posts, 
this was explicitly given at the end of the timestamp: the `Z` in `2024-12-16T18:42:03Z` 
means the 'plus zero' time zone, that is UTC or Greenwich Mean Time 
(also known as Zulu time, after the NATO alphabet pronunciation of the letter Z). 
You can check the current time zone of the timestamp column by calling `tz(posts$created_at)`.

Of course, since most of the posts will be from Brazil, it might be more appropriate to set it to 
Brazilian time using the `with_tz` function.
For example, the code below adds a version of the timestamp in Brazilian time,
and shows a line plot of hourly posts in both time zones:

```{webr}
#| exercise: with_tz
posts |> 
  mutate(
    created_br=with_tz(created_at, "America/Sao_Paulo"),
    hour_utc = hour(created_at),
    hour_br = hour(created_br)) |>
  ggplot() + 
  geom_line(aes(x=hour_utc, colour="UTC"), stat="count") +
  geom_line(aes(x=hour_br, colour="Brazil"), stat="count")+
  labs(x="Time of day", y="# of posts", colour="Time zone") + 
  theme_minimal()
```

As you can see, the Brasilia time zone is 3 hours behind UTC, 
placing most posts between 9:00 and 22:00 rather than the less plausible noon to after midnight. 

This example works because the data was explicitly given in the UTC time zone. 
Often, however, you might read data that implicitly assumes a local time zone.
In that case, you should tell R what the time zone is by using e.g. `timestamp=force_tz(timestamp, "Europe/Amsterdam")`.
So, use `with_tz` to change the time zone on a column that already has a correct time zone, 
and `force_tz` to tell R that the column is actually in a different time zone. 

### Dates in graphs

Although we will discuss visualization in more detail in @sec-vis and @sec-advancedggplot,
it is useful to know that ggplot handles dates and timestamps well by default.
This means that it will automatically use sensible names to place on an axis.
For example, when plotting the number of posts per week it will decide
that given the specific period, quarterly ticks make most sense:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ggplotdate
posts |> 
  mutate(week=floor_date(created_at, unit="week", week_start=1)) |>
  group_by(week) |>
  tally() |>
  ggplot(aes(x=week, y=n)) + geom_line() 
``` 

Note that you can change this default using scales:
try adding `+ scale_x_datetime(date_labels="%G-%V", date_breaks="4 weeks")` to the code above
(and see @sec-advancedggplot for a more in-depth explanation of ggplot scales)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Month and weekday names and locales"}

When dealing with month or weekday names, the results will of course be language-specific. 
By default, the formatting and parsing functions used above will use the local settings of the machine
the code is run on. You might have noticed that the graph above uses English month names in the browser.
If you run it on your own computer, it might use another language depending on your local settings.

If you only work with the language matching your local settings, this is probably fine:
R will automatically parse and format dates using the right month or day names.

However, if you are for example producing an English language report on a French-language computer,
you will probably prefer English names for the months. 
You can change the language settings in R using the `Sys.setlocale` command, 
which takes a locale identifier consisting (of the language, region, and encoding.
For example, `Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "nl_NL.UTF-8")` will set the date and time handling to Dutch,
while `Sys.setlocale("LC_TIME", "en_US.UTF-8")` will set it to US English.
Note that this setting will affect all subsequent R commands in this session,
and the locale does need to be installed on your system
(and in the interactive examples it does not do anything). 
Finally, locale strings are unfortunately different for different operating systems, 
so on Windows it will be called `Dutch_Netherlands` or `English_United States` instead. 

For parsing dates that use names in a different language from the computer's default,
it is also possible to use the `parse_date` and `parse_datetime` functions from the `readr` package
(included in `tidyverse`).
These functions take a format string with the same `%`-placeholders as discussed above,
as well as a `locale=` argument:

```{webr}
parse_date("3 août 2012", format="%d %B %Y", locale=locale('fr'))
```

`readr` ships with month and day names for almost 200 languages, so should work for most languages, 
including e.g. French and Swahili but also globally less relevant languages like my beloved Dutch.
:::
